title: An Introduction to Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST)
text:
An Introduction to Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) Author Akif Mustafa ✉ Published June 1, 2026 1 Introduction The Cox proportional hazards (CPH) model is the go-to model for survival analysis. It is popular for good reasons: It is semi-parametric — no distributional assumption needed. It handles multiple predictor variables. It gives an easy-to-interpret summary: the hazard ratio (HR) . It handles censoring naturally. But it makes one strong assumption: proportional hazards (PH) . This means the hazard of the event in two groups must always remain proportional throughout the study period. Everything works well when this holds. What if it does not hold? When hazards are not proportional — for example, when survival curves cross, when there is a delayed treatment effect, or when the benefit diminishes over time — a single HR becomes misleading. It no longer summarizes the treatment effect well. Potential hazard scenarious In these situations, there are several analytical alternatives to the standard Cox model: Piecewise Cox model Cox model with time-varying coefficients Royston-Parmar parametric model Accelerated failure time (AFT) model Cure models Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) is one such alternative. It is practical, interpretable, and widely used when the proportional hazards assumption is violated. 2 What is RMST? The Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) up to a time point \(	au\) is: The average time a person survives from time 0 to time \(	au\) . Equivalently, the area under the survival curve \(S(t)\) from 0 to \(	au\) . Mathematically: \[ 	ext{RMST}(	au) = E[\min(T, 	au)] = \int_0^{	au} S(t)\, dt \] Two key points: “Restricted” means we only look up to a pre-specified horizon \(	au\) (e.g., 5 years), not to infinity. It is a non-parametric summary of the whole survival curve up to \(	au\) . No proportional hazards assumption. No specific model required. 2.1 Visualizing RMST: Area Under the Curve Code set.seed ( 1 ) tau <- 48 t_seq <- seq ( 0 , 60 , by = 0.1 ) s_t <- exp ( - 0.03 * t_seq) df_line <- data.frame ( time = t_seq, surv = s_t) df_shade <- data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , t_seq[t_seq <= tau], tau), surv = c ( 0 , s_t[t_seq <= tau], 0 ) ) ggplot () + geom_polygon ( data = df_shade, aes (time, surv), fill = "steelblue" , alpha = 0.35 ) + geom_line ( data = df_line, aes (time, surv), color = "steelblue" , linewidth = 1.2 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau + 1.5 , y = 0.85 , label = expression (tau), size = 5 , hjust = 0 ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau / 2.5 , y = 0.22 , label = "RMST = Area 
 under S(t) 
 up to τ" , size = 3.8 , color = "steelblue4" , fontface = "bold" ) + labs ( title = "Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST)" , subtitle = paste0 ( "Shaded area = RMST up to τ = " , tau, " months" ), x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + scale_x_continuous ( breaks = seq ( 0 , 60 , 12 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) RMST is the area under the survival curve S(t) from time 0 to τ 2.2 RMST for Two Groups For two groups (e.g., treatment vs. control), the difference in RMST is the area between the two survival curves from 0 to \(	au\) . It tells you: on average, how much extra survival time does the treatment provide up to time \(	au\) ? Code set.seed ( 2 ) tau <- 48 t_seq <- seq ( 0 , 60 , by = 0.1 ) s_trt <- exp ( - 0.020 * t_seq) s_ctrl <- exp ( - 0.035 * t_seq) df_two <- data.frame ( time = t_seq, Treated = s_trt, Control = s_ctrl ) |> tidyr :: pivot_longer ( - time, names_to = "Group" , values_to = "Survival" ) df_between <- data.frame ( time = c (t_seq[t_seq <= tau], rev (t_seq[t_seq <= tau])), surv = c (s_trt[t_seq <= tau], rev (s_ctrl[t_seq <= tau])) ) ggplot () + geom_polygon ( data = df_between, aes (time, surv), fill = "gold" , alpha = 0.5 ) + geom_line ( data = df_two, aes (time, Survival, color = Group), linewidth = 1.2 ) + geom_vline ( xintercept = tau, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau + 1.5 , y = 0.9 , label = expression (tau), size = 5 , hjust = 0 ) + annotate ( "text" , x = 15 , y = 0.55 , label = "RMST 
 Difference" , size = 3.8 , color = "darkgoldenrod" , fontface = "bold" ) + scale_color_manual ( values = c ( "Control" = "tomato" , "Treated" = "steelblue" )) + labs ( title = "RMST Difference Between Two Groups" , subtitle = "Shaded area = difference in RMST up to τ" , x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + scale_x_continuous ( breaks = seq ( 0 , 60 , 12 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) RMST difference = shaded area between the two survival curves up to τ 3 Why RMST? Limitations of the Cox Model The Cox model gives hazard ratios. HRs are useful, but they have real limitations. 3.1 PH Assumption The Cox model requires proportional hazards . If hazards are not proportional (crossing curves, delayed effects, diminishing benefits), a single HR is misleading. In immuno-oncology, for example, survival curves often separate late or cross altogether. The PH assumption frequently fails here. 3.2 HR is Relative, Not Absolute HR = 0.6 means a 40% lower hazard. But what does that mean in months of life gained ? That depends on the baseline hazard — a detail HR does not convey. Clinicians and patients often more interested in: “How much extra time do I get, on average?” than about a hazard ratio. 3.3 HR is Model-Based The Cox HR is a model-based summary. If the model is wrong — due to non-proportional hazards or misspecification — the HR can be biased and difficult to interpret. 3.4 How RMST Addresses These Limitations Issue Cox HR RMST Requires PH assumption ✅ Yes ❌ No Absolute effect size ❌ No ✅ Yes (time gained) Model-free ❌ No ✅ Yes (from KM curve) Easy clinical communication ⚠️ Moderate ✅ High RMST is not a replacement for the Cox model in all settings. It is a complement and an alternative — especially when PH fails or an absolute effect size matters more. 4 When to Use RMST? 4.1 Use RMST When: 1. Non-proportional hazards (NPH) are present Crossing survival curves Delayed treatment effect (early overlap, later separation) Diminishing benefit (early benefit that later fades) 2. An absolute effect is more meaningful than a relative one “Patients in the active arm survive on average 3 months longer over 5 years.” Health economics: quantifying life-years gained within a fixed horizon. 3. You want a model-free summary No reliance on a correctly specified Cox model. Simple, robust comparison of two survival curves up to \(	au\) . 4. As a supplement to HRs and log-rank tests Even when PH holds, RMST can be reported alongside the HR to provide an absolute effect estimate. Many recent clinical trials in oncology report both HR and RMST difference. 4.2 You Probably Do Not Need RMST When: PH holds well, and HR is sufficient for your scientific or clinical question, and There is no strong demand for an absolute “time gained” interpretation. 5 Estimation 5.1 Single Group The steps are straightforward: Estimate the survival curve \(S(t)\) using the Kaplan–Meier estimator. Choose a clinically relevant truncation time \(	au\) (e.g., 5 years). Pre-specify this before the analysis. Compute the area under the KM curve from 0 to \(	au\) using the trapezoidal rule (sum of rectangles under the step function). Estimate the standard error using a Greenwood-type formula. Construct confidence intervals using asymptotic normality (for large samples). 5.2 Two-Group Comparison Let \(S_1(t)\) and \(S_0(t)\) be the KM curves in the treatment and control groups. \[ 	ext{RMST}_1(	au) = \int_0^{	au} S_1(t)\, dt \qquad 	ext{RMST}_0(	au) = \int_0^{	au} S_0(t)\, dt \] Three key summary measures: 1. Difference in RMST (most common) \[ \Delta(	au) = 	ext{RMST}_1(	au) - 	ext{RMST}_0(	au) = \int_0^{	au} [S_1(t) - S_0(t)]\, dt \] Interpretation : On average, how many extra months does treatment provide by time \(	au\) ? 2. Ratio of RMST \[  rac{	ext{RMST}_1(	au)}{	ext{RMST}_0(	au)} \] Interpretation : Relative increase in average survival time up to \(	au\) . 3. Ratio of Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) \[ 	ext{RMTL}(	au) = 	au - 	ext{RMST}(	au) \] This is the average time lost due to the event before \(	au\) . \[ 	ext{RMTL ratio} =  rac{	ext{RMTL}_1(	au)}{	ext{RMTL}_0(	au)} \] Interpretation : Useful when the focus is on time lost rather than time lived. Inference (difference and ratio): Based on asymptotic normality with Greenwood-based variance estimates. Provides standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values. 6 Choosing \(	au\) The choice of \(	au\) matters. Some guidance: \(	au\) should be clinically chosen and pre-specified before the analysis (e.g., 5-year RMST in a cancer trial). It must fall within the observed follow-up where enough events have occurred and the KM estimate is reliable (i.e., do not extrapolate beyond the last event time). A common practical rule: set \(	au\) at or before the minimum of the two groups’ last event times , or at a clinically meaningful landmark such as 1, 2, or 5 years. Some methods choose \(	au\) adaptively, but a fixed, pre-specified \(	au\) is preferred for transparency and interpretability. Effect of τ choice on RMST estimation. The shaded areas show RMST for three different values of τ. 7 Example in R Here we simulate a delayed treatment effect: Before 12 months: treatment and control have similar hazard. After 12 months: treatment hazard becomes lower. This violates proportional hazards. 7.1 Simulate Data Code library (survival) library (survRM2) library (ggplot2) library (dplyr) library (tibble) library (knitr) library (kableExtra) set.seed ( 999 ) n <- 600 arm <- rbinom (n, 1 , 0.5 ) # 0 = control, 1 = treatment # Control: constant hazard throughout t_control <- rexp (n, rate = 0.05 ) # Treatment: same hazard before 12 months, lower hazard after 12 months t1 <- rexp (n, rate = 0.05 ) t_treat <- ifelse (t1 < 12 , t1, 12 + rexp (n, rate = 0.02 )) time_event <- ifelse (arm == 0 , t_control, t_treat) # Administrative censoring at 36 months time <- pmin (time_event, 36 ) status <- as.integer (time_event <= 36 ) dat <- tibble ( time = time, status = status, arm = factor (arm, levels = c ( 0 , 1 ), labels = c ( "Control" , "Treatment" )) ) # Summary table dat |> group_by (arm) |> summarise ( N = n (), Events = sum (status), Censored = N - Events, Max_followup = round ( max (time), 1 ), .groups = "drop" ) |> kable ( caption = "Summary of simulated dataset" , col.names = c ( "Group" , "N" , "Events" , "Censored" , "Max Follow-up (months)" ) ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) Summary of simulated dataset Group N Events Censored Max Follow-up (months) Control 302 248 54 36 Treatment 298 208 90 36 7.2 Kaplan–Meier Curves Code fit_km <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) # Extract KM step data for ggplot km_df <- data.frame ( time = fit_km $ time, surv = fit_km $ surv, strata = rep ( names (fit_km $ strata), fit_km $ strata) ) |> mutate ( arm = sub ( "arm=" , "" , strata)) # Add time = 0 rows for each group time0 <- data.frame ( time = 0 , surv = 1 , strata = NA , arm = c ( "Control" , "Treatment" ) ) km_plot_df <- bind_rows (time0, km_df) |> arrange (arm, time) ggplot (km_plot_df, aes ( x = time, y = surv, color = arm)) + geom_step ( linewidth = 1 ) + scale_color_manual ( name = "Group" , values = c ( "Control" = "tomato" , "Treatment" = "steelblue" ) ) + scale_x_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 36 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 36 , 6 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + labs ( title = "Kaplan–Meier Curves: Delayed Treatment Effect" , subtitle = "Curves overlap early and diverge after ~12 months" , x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability" ) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) Kaplan–Meier curves for simulated delayed treatment effect data The curves initially overlap, reflecting similar early hazards. After 12 months they diverge as the treatment arm benefits from a lower hazard. This pattern suggests a violation of the proportional hazards assumption. 7.3 Check the Proportional Hazards Assumption 7.3.1 First, lets fit the cox PH model Code cox_fit <- coxph ( Surv (time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) summary (cox_fit) Call: coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ arm, data = dat) n= 600, number of events= 456 coef exp(coef) se(coef) z Pr(>|z|) armTreatment -0.23982 0.78677 0.09429 -2.543 0.011 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95 armTreatment 0.7868 1.271 0.654 0.9465 Concordance= 0.518 (se = 0.013 ) Likelihood ratio test= 6.5 on 1 df, p=0.01 Wald test = 6.47 on 1 df, p=0.01 Score (logrank) test = 6.5 on 1 df, p=0.01 7.3.2 Now, check the PH assumption using schoenfeld test Code zph <- cox.zph (cox_fit) # Print test result as a neat table as.data.frame (zph $ table) |> kable ( caption = "Schoenfeld residuals test for proportional hazards" , digits = 4 ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) Schoenfeld residuals test for proportional hazards chisq df p arm 8.4937 1 0.0036 GLOBAL 8.4937 1 0.0036 A p-value below 0.05 on the Schoenfeld test indicates a violation of the PH assumption. 7.3.3 Plot the Schoenfeld residuals for visual inspection Code plot (zph, main = "Schoenfeld Residuals Over Time" ) abline ( h = 0 , lty = 2 , col = "grey50" ) Scaled Schoenfeld residuals. A flat line suggests PH holds; a trend suggests violation. A non-linear trend in the residuals plot confirms this. PH is violated here — making RMST a better choice. 7.4 Compute RMST We use the survRM2 package and set \(	au = 36\) months. Code tau_val <- 36 rm <- rmst2 ( time = dat $ time, status = dat $ status, arm = as.integer (dat $ arm == "Treatment" ), # 1 = treatment, 0 = control tau = tau_val ) rm The truncation time: tau = 36 was specified. Restricted Mean Survival Time (RMST) by arm Est. se lower .95 upper .95 RMST (arm=1) 18.613 0.804 17.038 20.189 RMST (arm=0) 16.722 0.716 15.319 18.125 Restricted Mean Time Lost (RMTL) by arm Est. se lower .95 upper .95 RMTL (arm=1) 17.387 0.804 15.811 18.962 RMTL (arm=0) 19.278 0.716 17.875 20.681 Between-group contrast Est. lower .95 upper .95 p RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0) 1.891 -0.218 4.001 0.079 RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0) 1.113 0.988 1.254 0.078 RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0) 0.902 0.803 1.013 0.082 7.4.1 Results Tables Code arm1_vec <- unlist (rm $ RMST.arm1) arm0_vec <- unlist (rm $ RMST.arm0) rmst_trt_est <- as.numeric (arm1_vec[ 1 ]) rmst_trt_lo <- as.numeric (arm1_vec[ 2 ]) rmst_trt_hi <- as.numeric (arm1_vec[ 3 ]) rmst_ctrl_est <- as.numeric (arm0_vec[ 1 ]) rmst_ctrl_lo <- as.numeric (arm0_vec[ 2 ]) rmst_ctrl_hi <- as.numeric (arm0_vec[ 3 ]) rmst_summary <- data.frame ( Group = c ( "Treatment" , "Control" ), RMST = c (rmst_trt_est, rmst_ctrl_est), Lower = c (rmst_trt_lo, rmst_ctrl_lo), Upper = c (rmst_trt_hi, rmst_ctrl_hi) ) rmst_summary |> kable ( caption = paste0 ( "RMST estimates up to τ = " , tau_val, " months" ), col.names = c ( "Group" , "RMST (months)" , "95% CI Lower" , "95% CI Upper" ), digits = 2 ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) RMST estimates up to τ = 36 months Group RMST (months) 95% CI Lower 95% CI Upper Treatment 18.61 17.39 0.80 Control 16.72 19.28 0.72 7.4.2 Contrast Table Code contrast_df <- as.data.frame (rm $ unadjusted.result) contrast_df $ Measure <- c ( "RMST Difference (Treatment - Control)" , "RMST Ratio (Treatment / Control)" , "RMTL Ratio (Treatment / Control)" ) contrast_df <- contrast_df[, c ( "Measure" , "Est." , "lower .95" , "upper .95" , "p" )] contrast_df |> kable ( caption = "RMST contrast measures" , col.names = c ( "Measure" , "Estimate" , "95% CI Lower" , "95% CI Upper" , "P-value" ), digits = c ( 0 , 2 , 2 , 2 , 4 ) ) |> kable_styling ( bootstrap_options = c ( "striped" , "hover" , "condensed" ), full_width = FALSE ) RMST contrast measures Measure Estimate 95% CI Lower 95% CI Upper P-value RMST (arm=1)-(arm=0) RMST Difference (Treatment - Control) 1.89 -0.22 4.00 0.0789 RMST (arm=1)/(arm=0) RMST Ratio (Treatment / Control) 1.11 0.99 1.25 0.0780 RMTL (arm=1)/(arm=0) RMTL Ratio (Treatment / Control) 0.90 0.80 1.01 0.0816 7.5 Visualize RMST Code # Fit separate KM curves for each arm km_trt <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ 1 , data = filter (dat, arm == "Treatment" )) km_ctrl <- survfit ( Surv (time, status) ~ 1 , data = filter (dat, arm == "Control" )) # Helper: convert survfit object to a step-function data frame km_to_df <- function (km_obj, group_label) { data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , km_obj $ time), surv = c ( 1 , km_obj $ surv), group = group_label ) } df_trt <- km_to_df (km_trt, "Treatment" ) df_ctrl <- km_to_df (km_ctrl, "Control" ) # Helper: build a closed polygon for shading up to tau make_shade <- function (df, tau_limit) { # Keep only time points up to tau df_trunc <- df[df $ time <= tau_limit, ] # Add a closing point at tau with the last survival value df_trunc <- rbind (df_trunc, data.frame ( time = tau_limit, surv = tail (df_trunc $ surv, 1 ), group = df_trunc $ group[ 1 ])) # Close the polygon back to zero data.frame ( time = c ( 0 , df_trunc $ time, tau_limit, 0 ), surv = c ( 0 , df_trunc $ surv, 0 , 0 ), group = df_trunc $ group[ 1 ] ) } shade_trt <- make_shade (df_trt, tau_val) shade_ctrl <- make_shade (df_ctrl, tau_val) ggplot () + # Shaded RMST areas geom_polygon ( data = shade_trt, aes (time, surv), fill = "steelblue" , alpha = 0.25 ) + geom_polygon ( data = shade_ctrl, aes (time, surv), fill = "tomato" , alpha = 0.25 ) + # KM step curves geom_step ( data = df_trt, aes (time, surv, color = "Treatment" ), linewidth = 1 ) + geom_step ( data = df_ctrl, aes (time, surv, color = "Control" ), linewidth = 1 ) + # Tau line geom_vline ( xintercept = tau_val, linetype = "dashed" , color = "black" ) + annotate ( "text" , x = tau_val - 1 , y = 0.05 , label = paste0 ( "τ = " , tau_val, " months" ), hjust = 1 , size = 3.5 ) + scale_color_manual ( name = "Group" , values = c ( "Treatment" = "cyan3" , "Control" = "tomato" ) ) + scale_x_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 36 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 36 , 6 )) + scale_y_continuous ( limits = c ( 0 , 1 ), breaks = seq ( 0 , 1 , 0.2 )) + labs ( title = "RMST Visualization: KM Curves with Shaded Areas" , subtitle = paste0 ( "Shaded area = RMST up to τ = " , tau_val, " months" ), x = "Time (months)" , y = "Survival probability S(t)" ) + theme_classic ( base_size = 12 ) + theme ( legend.position = "bottom" ) KM curves with shaded RMST areas up to τ = 36 months 7.6 Interpretation Key Results Treatment group : RMST = 19 months up to \(	au\) = 36 months. Control group : RMST = 17 months up to \(	au\) = 36 months. RMST Difference : 1.9 months (95% CI: -0.22 to 4.001; p = 0.0789). Plain language : On average, patients in the treatment group survive 1.9 months longer within the first 36 months compared to the control group. This is a clinically meaningful and model-free summary of the treatment benefit — no proportional hazards assumption required. 8 References Uno H, et al. (2014). (2016). Comparison of treatment effects measured by the hazard ratio and by the ratio of restricted mean survival times in oncology randomized controlled trials. Journal of Clinical Oncology .
